title: Equilibrium of aggregate demand and aggregate supply
competency: Find short-run and long-run equilibrium and explain the effects of demand and supply shocks on the price level and real GDP.

keywords.def: The price level and real GDP at which real GDP demanded equals real GDP supplied: where AD meets AS.
The point where AD crosses SRAS, giving Pₑ and Qₑ.
Quantity of real GDP supplied is greater than quantity demanded (price level above Pₑ).
Quantity of real GDP demanded is greater than quantity supplied (price level below Pₑ).

en.text: Short-run equilibrium is where AD crosses SRAS: real GDP demanded equals real GDP supplied, at price level Pₑ and output Qₑ. Above Pₑ there is a surplus, so the price level falls; below Pₑ there is a shortage, so it rises. In long-run (static) equilibrium AD, SRAS and LRAS meet at one point, at natural real GDP, and the economy stays there while the curves do not shift.

am.text: የአጭር ጊዜ ሚዛን AD እና SRAS በሚገናኙበት ነው። ከPₑ በላይ ትርፍ ምርት፣ ከPₑ በታች እጥረት አለ። በረጅም ጊዜ ሚዛን AD፣ SRAS እና LRAS በአንድ ነጥብ ይገናኛሉ።

screens.title: Move the curves
screens.ask: A linear AS–AD model: AD is Qd = a − 200P, SRAS is Qs = c + 200P. Raise a (more spending), then lower c (less supply). Which way does the price level move each time?
screens.note: Real GDP = (a + c) ÷ 2. Start: price level 2, real GDP 600 billion Birr. Numbers are added for practice.

screens.title: Short-run equilibrium
paras: AD and SRAS together set the price level and real GDP.
Figure 2.6 compares three price levels: P₁, Pₑ and P₂.
At P₁ (high): supplied Q₂ > demanded Q₁. Surplus. The price level falls.
At P₂ (low): demanded Q₂ > supplied Q₁. Shortage. The price level rises.
Both push the economy to E, where demanded = supplied.
Pₑ is the equilibrium price level; Qₑ is equilibrium real GDP.

screens.title: Static (long-run) equilibrium
paras: Short run: AD meets SRAS.
Long run: AD meets LRAS.
Figure 2.7: AD, SRAS and LRAS meet at one point.
Output is at the natural rate, at the equilibrium price.
If the curves do not shift, the economy stays there indefinitely.

screens.title: Worked example: a linear AS–AD model
steps: At P = 2.5: Qd = 500, Qs = 700 → surplus of 200 → P falls.
At P = 1.5: Qd = 700, Qs = 500 → shortage of 200 → P rises.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Macroeconomic equilibrium
The price level and real GDP at which real GDP demanded equals real GDP supplied: where AD meets AS.
Short-run equilibrium
The point where AD crosses SRAS, giving Pₑ and Qₑ.
Surplus
Quantity of real GDP supplied is greater than quantity demanded (price level above Pₑ).
Shortage
Quantity of real GDP demanded is greater than quantity supplied (price level below Pₑ).
Static equilibrium

screens.text: At a price level above Pₑ there is
opts: a surplus, so the price level falls
a shortage, so the price level rises
a surplus, so the price level rises
screens.ans: a surplus, so the price level falls
screens.why: Above Pₑ, supply exceeds demand (Figure 2.6 at P₁): prices fall, firms cut output, buyers buy more.
screens.clue: Compare supplied and demanded at a high price.
Set Qd = Qs and collect the P terms.

With Qd = 1000 − 200P and Qs = 200 + 200P, at P = 3 the surplus is ___ billion Birr
screens.clue: Work out Qd and Qs at P = 3.

screens.text: At long-run equilibrium, AD, SRAS and LRAS all meet at one point.
screens.why: Figure 2.7 shows all three curves crossing at natural real GDP.

screens.title: What happens when the price level is below Pₑ?
items: Firms raise output and buyers buy less
screens.why: p.42: a shortage pushes the price level up until demanded = supplied.
screens.clue: Start with comparing demand and supply.

screens.ask: AD: Qd = 1200 − 100P. SRAS: Qs = 300 + 200P. Equilibrium real GDP Qₑ = ___ billion Birr

en.text: A demand shock is an unexpected shift of the AD curve, for example from expansionary monetary or fiscal policy or a rise in desired spending. An expansionary shock shifts AD right and raises both the price level and real GDP; a contractionary shock shifts AD left and lowers both. Demand shocks move P and Y in the same direction.

am.text: የፍላጎት ድንገተኛ ለውጥ AD ኩርባን ያንቀሳቅሳል። AD ወደ ቀኝ ሲሄድ ዋጋና ምርት ሁለቱም ይጨምራሉ፤ ወደ ግራ ሲሄድ ሁለቱም ይቀንሳሉ።

screens.title: Add or cut spending
screens.ask: Same model: Qd = 1000 + g − 200P, Qs = 200 + 200P. Add or remove spending g at every price level (like a change in G). Does real GDP move the same way as the price level?
screens.note: The price level = 2 + g ÷ 400. Both rise when g rises and both fall when g falls.

screens.title: Demand shocks
paras: A demand shock is an unexpected shift of the AD curve.
Causes: expansionary monetary policy, expansionary fiscal policy, or more desired spending.
Expansionary shock: AD shifts right; P and Y both rise.
Contractionary shock: AD shifts left; P and Y both fall.
"Expansionary" and "contractionary" describe the effect on equilibrium output.

screens.title: Figure 2.8
paras: AD₀ meets AS at E₀ (Y₀, P₀).
AD shifts right to AD₁.
New equilibrium E₁ (Y₁, P₁): Y₁ > Y₀ and P₁ > P₀.
Demand shocks move P and Y in the same direction.

screens.title: Worked example: government spending rises
steps: G adds 200 at every price level: Qd = 1200 − 200P.
P rises 2 → 2.5 and Y rises 600 → 700: same direction.
Y rises by 100, not 200: higher prices absorb part of the shift.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Demand shock
An unexpected shift of the AD curve; it moves the price level and real GDP in the same direction.
Expansionary shock
A shock that raises equilibrium output (e.g. AD shifts right).
Contractionary shock
A shock that lowers equilibrium output (e.g. AD shifts left).

screens.text: An expansionary demand shock makes the price level and real GDP
screens.why: AD shifts right along an upward SRAS (Figure 2.8).

pool: Foreign incomes fall, so exports fall
a: Foreign incomes fall, so exports fall
screens.why: These change spending (G, C, X), so AD shifts. Drought and oil prices change costs and supply.
screens.clue: Does it change spending or production costs?

screens.ask: Start: Qd = 1000 − 200P, Qs = 200 + 200P. Spending falls by 200 at every price level (Qd = 800 − 200P). New price level = ___
screens.clue: Set the new Qd equal to Qs.

screens.ask: In that case (Qd = 800 − 200P, Qs = 200 + 200P) new real GDP = ___ billion Birr
screens.why: Q = 200 + 200 × 1.5 = 500. P and Y both fell: a contractionary demand shock.

screens.text: A contractionary demand shock lowers both the price level and real GDP.
screens.why: AD shifts left: P ↓ and Y ↓.
screens.clue: Demand shocks move P and Y together.

screens.text: In the worked example, AD shifted right by 200 but real GDP rose by only 100. Why?
opts: Part of the shift raised the price level instead of output
Government spending does not count in AD
SRAS shifted left at the same time
screens.ans: Part of the shift raised the price level instead of output
screens.why: Along an upward SRAS, the higher price level cuts quantity demanded, so output rises less than the shift.

en.text: A supply shock shifts the SRAS curve and moves the price level and real GDP in opposite directions. Better technology or more labour or capital shifts SRAS right: P falls and Y rises. A storm that destroys crops or a rise in the price of oil shifts SRAS left: P rises and Y falls, which is called stagflation (Figure 2.9).

am.text: የአቅርቦት ድንገተኛ ለውጥ ዋጋና ምርትን በተቃራኒ አቅጣጫ ያንቀሳቅሳል። የነዳጅ ዋጋ ሲጨምር ዋጋ ይጨምራል፣ ምርት ይቀንሳል።

screens.title: Oil price jump
screens.ask: The world price of oil suddenly doubles. Ethiopia imports all its fuel. What happens to the price level and real GDP?
screens.after: Costs rise, so SRAS shifts left: prices up, output down. Supply shocks move P and Y in opposite directions.

screens.title: Supply shocks
paras: Supply shocks move P and Y in opposite directions.
Positive: better technology, more labour or capital → SRAS right.
Negative: a storm destroys crops, or imported inputs like oil are cut off → SRAS left.
Example: the price of oil rises; SRAS₁ shifts left to SRAS₂.
Equilibrium moves from A (Y₁, P₁) to B (Y₂, P₂): output falls, price level rises (Figure 2.9).

screens.title: Comparing shocks
paras: Demand shocks: same direction. Supply shocks: opposite directions.

screens.title: Worked example: an oil price shock
steps: Oil cuts supply by 200 at every price level: Qs = 200P.
P rises 2 → 2.5 while Y falls 600 → 500: opposite directions.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Supply shock
An unexpected shift of the AS curve; it moves the price level and real GDP in opposite directions.
Stagflation
A rising price level together with falling output, as after a negative supply shock.

opts: a higher price level and lower output
a lower price level and higher output
a higher price level and higher output
a lower price level and lower output
screens.ans: a higher price level and lower output
screens.why: SRAS shifts left along a fixed AD (Figure 2.9, A → B).
screens.clue: Supply shocks move P and Y in opposite directions.

screens.title: Demand shock or supply shock?
screens.why: Spending changes shift AD; cost, resource and technology changes shift SRAS.

screens.title: Match each shock with its effect
screens.why: Demand: same direction. Supply: opposite directions.
screens.clue: Which curve moves, and which way?

screens.ask: Start: Qd = 1000 − 200P, Qs = 200 + 200P. New technology adds 200 to supply (Qs = 400 + 200P). New price level = ___
screens.why: 1000 − 200P = 400 + 200P → 600 = 400P → P = 1.5; Q = 700. P falls, Y rises: a positive supply shock.
screens.clue: Set Qd equal to the new Qs.

screens.text: Spot the mistake. The book says an oil shock causes "an increase in price from Y₁ to Y₂". It should say
opts: an increase in the price level from P₁ to P₂
an increase in output from Y₁ to Y₂
a fall in the price level from P₂ to P₁
screens.ans: an increase in the price level from P₁ to P₂
screens.why: Y is output and P is the price level. In Figure 2.9 output falls Y₁ → Y₂ and the price level rises P₁ → P₂.
screens.clue: Which letter stands for the price level?

screens.text: Ethiopian prices rise and real GDP falls at the same time. Which event best explains this?
opts: The Birr depreciates and exports rise
screens.why: P ↑ with Y ↓ is the sign of a negative supply shock (stagflation). The other three shift AD right and raise both P and Y.
screens.clue: Opposite directions point to which kind of shock?

notes.text: p.44: "an increase in price from Y₁ to Y₂" should be "an increase in the price level from P₁ to P₂", and "shift … from SRAS" should be "from SRAS₁ to SRAS₂". The text never cites Figure 2.9, which it describes.

p.42: "how the market price of a product is determined" should be "how the general price level and real GDP are determined". Figure 2.6 labels the AD curve "Short-run Aggregate Demand"; there is only one AD curve.
The linear model (Qd = 1000 − 200P, Qs = 200 + 200P), its shocks, both sliders and the numeric items are added for practice; they follow the book's figures.
